title: Where Does a Seabird's Salt Go?

scenes.visual: Title card 'Where Does a Seabird's Salt Go?' over a cormorant silhouette on a rock above waves. Reuses the first film's COLOUR MAP: water BLUE, sodium chloride ORANGE dots, outlines charcoal; DASHED arrow = passive leak, SOLID arrow with 'ATP' tag = paid transport. The first film's two-column 'In / Out' ledger and corner osmolality bar return. Every number appears only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: A cormorant at sea has salt water all around. Its kidneys cannot make urine as salty as the sea, so where does its extra salt go?
scenes.visual: A cormorant dives through BLUE water speckled with ORANGE dots and surfaces with a fish. A kidney icon beside it with a bar that stops below a 'seawater' tick. Question mark over the bird.
scenes.narration: A cormorant at sea has salt water all around. Its kidneys cannot make urine as salty as the sea, so where does its extra salt go?

scenes.tts: The first film balanced a fish's water and salt in a ledger of gains and losses. A sea fish pumps its extra salt out across its gills. A bird has no gills.
scenes.visual: Brief replay: the first film's SEA fish with SOLID ORANGE 'ATP' arrows leaving its gills and a balanced ledger. The fish outline morphs into the cormorant outline; the gill arrows fade away and the ledger's ORANGE 'Out' row goes empty and red.
scenes.narration: The first film balanced a fish's water and salt in a ledger of gains and losses. A sea fish pumps its extra salt out across its gills. A bird has no gills.

scenes.tts: Clearing seawater's salt through its kidneys alone would cost the bird more water than it drank. The ledger cannot balance that way. Is there another route out?
scenes.visual: Ledger beside the cormorant. A BLUE 'In' bar labelled 'seawater, if it drank some'. A BLUE 'Out' bar labelled 'urine needed to carry its salt' grows longer than the 'In' bar; the water row flashes red. A dotted outline of a second exit, labelled '?', appears on the bird's head.
scenes.narration: Clearing seawater's salt through its kidneys alone would cost the bird more water than it drank. The ledger cannot balance that way. Is there another route out?

scenes.tts: Knut Schmidt Nielsen, C. B. Yorgensen and H. Osaki tested that question. They worked with double crested cormorants.
scenes.caption: Knut Schmidt-Nielsen, C. B. Jørgensen and H. Osaki tested that question. They worked with double-crested cormorants.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Schmidt-Nielsen, Jørgensen and Osaki, 1958'. A cartoon lab bench with a cormorant standing in a padded holder. No portraits.
scenes.narration: Knut Schmidt-Nielsen, C. B. Jørgensen and H. Osaki tested that question. They worked with double-crested cormorants.

scenes.tts: They gave the birds a load of salt, by mouth or by infusion. Then they collected two separate fluids from each bird, and compared them.
scenes.visual: A flask of ORANGE-speckled salt solution with a tube to the bird's bill (label 'by mouth'), and a second thin line to a wing vein (label 'or by infusion'). ORANGE dots spread through the bird's body outline.
scenes.narration: They gave the birds a load of salt, by mouth or by infusion. Then they collected two separate fluids from each bird, and compared them.

scenes.tts: One vial caught fluid from the cloaca, which is urine mixed with feces. The other caught a clear fluid that dripped from the tip of the beak.
scenes.visual: Two empty vials appear: one under the beak tip labelled 'beak drip', one under the vent labelled 'cloacal fluid (urine + feces)'. Beside them, a vertical salt-concentration bar (sodium, not osmolality) with a BLUE tick marked 'seawater sodium'.
scenes.narration: One vial caught fluid from the cloaca, which is urine mixed with feces. The other caught a clear fluid that dripped from the tip of the beak.

scenes.tts: Before the results, make a guess. Which vial do you think will be the saltier one?
scenes.visual: Both vials glow with question marks beside the shared sodium-concentration bar. Question card: 'which vial is saltier?'
scenes.narration: Before the results, make a guess. Which vial do you think will be the saltier one?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: If the kidney route ran saltier, the cloacal vial would plot higher. Instead, the beak vial filled with a concentrated salt solution. The cloacal fluid stayed much less salty.
scenes.visual: Clear fluid drips from the beak tip into the beak vial; it fills densely with ORANGE dots. The cloacal vial fills with sparse ORANGE dots. Each vial's ORANGE level is plotted on the shared sodium-concentration bar. Label: 'concentrations only: not the amount each route carried'.
scenes.narration: If the kidney route ran saltier, the cloacal vial would plot higher. Instead, the beak vial filled with a concentrated salt solution. The cloacal fluid stayed much less salty.

scenes.tts: On the bar, the beak fluid reached about the level of seawater, or somewhat more. And the glands made it fast. Steady secretion could clear the body's salt within hours.
scenes.visual: On the salt-concentration bar, the beak vial's ORANGE level rises to the BLUE 'seawater sodium' tick and a little past it, label 'about seawater or somewhat more'; the cloacal level stays far below. A clock face sweeps to '~10 h' while the ORANGE dots inside the bird's outline drain away through the beak.
scenes.narration: On the bar, the beak fluid reached about the level of seawater, or somewhat more. And the glands made it fast. Steady secretion could clear the body's salt within hours.

scenes.tts: The fluid came from paired glands in the head, the nasal salt glands. It ran out through the internal nostrils inside the mouth, and dripped from the tip of the beak.
scenes.visual: Cut-away of the cormorant's head (schematic): two gland lobes in the head, a duct running forward from each into the nasal cavity, fluid passing out through the internal nostrils inside the mouth and dripping from the beak tip. Label 'nasal salt glands (schematic)'.
scenes.narration: The fluid came from paired glands in the head, the nasal salt glands. It ran out through the internal nostrils inside the mouth, and dripped from the tip of the beak.

scenes.tts: Back to the ledger. Getting rid of salt costs water. The saltier the gland fluid, the less water each bit of salt takes with it.
scenes.visual: Ledger returns, but with no amount bars. Instead, a simple line chart: x-axis 'secretion concentration', y-axis 'water cost per unit of salt', a line falling from left to right; ticks for 'cloacal fluid', 'seawater sodium' and 'beak fluid'. Label 'water cost per mole of NaCl falls as secretion concentration rises'. Footnote card: 'whole-bird balance also needs the volume and makeup of every input and output (not measured here)'.
scenes.narration: Back to the ledger. Getting rid of salt costs water. The saltier the gland fluid, the less water each bit of salt takes with it.

scenes.tts: Gulls reach higher salt levels still. In a later experiment on a gull, the salt gland removed many times as much salt as the cloaca.
scenes.visual: A gull silhouette replaces the cormorant. Two ORANGE bars beside it: 'salt gland' about ten times as tall as 'cloaca', on-screen text '~10x'. Caption 'Schmidt-Nielsen, described 1960'.
scenes.narration: Gulls reach higher salt levels still. In a later experiment on a gull, the salt gland removed many times as much salt as the cloaca.

scenes.tts: The experiment showed a second route for salt, one that bypasses the kidney. It did not show how the gland concentrates salt, or that every bird has one.
scenes.visual: Two cards. Green check card: 'shown: an extrarenal route that clears a salt load'. Grey card with two question marks: 'not shown: how the gland concentrates salt' and 'not shown: that every bird has active salt glands'.
scenes.narration: The experiment showed a second route for salt, one that bypasses the kidney. It did not show how the gland concentrates salt, or that every bird has one.

scenes.tts: The bookkeeping is the same as the fish's. The bird's second route out is a gland, and how salty it runs sets the water cost.
scenes.visual: The fish ledger from the first film and the bird's concentration chart slide side by side. Under the fish: 'route out: gills'. Under the bird: 'route out: salt glands; volumes not measured'.
scenes.narration: The bookkeeping is the same as the fish's. The bird's second route out is a gland, and how salty it runs sets the water cost.

scenes.visual: End card with the Hex mascot beside a cormorant with a drop at its beak tip. Take-home line: 'A more concentrated salt secretion costs less water per unit salt.'
